```{python}
#| label: ldn-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ldn_att = pd.read_csv("examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
ldn_top = ldn_att.loc[ldn_att["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
ldn_top_name = ldn_top["attraction"]
ldn_top_short = ldn_top_name.split(" (")[0]
ldn_top_visits = f"{ldn_top['visits_2025']:,}"
ldn_total = f"{ldn_att['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
ldn_n = len(ldn_att)
ldn_n_free = int(ldn_att["admission"].str.startswith("Free").sum())
ldn_entry = "Free to enter" if ldn_top["admission"].startswith("Free") else "Tickets needed"
```

::: {.notes}
Part 1 audience: newcomers to Quarto. Objective: one Markdown guide becomes HTML, Word,

## 📜 AGENTS.md: rules the assistant reads {#agents-md}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🎯]{.big}

**Scope**

what the project is, and is not
:::
::: {}
[📏]{.big}

**Rules**

what must always hold
:::
::: {}
[⌨️]{.big}

**Commands**

how to build and check it
:::
::: {}
[🔁]{.big}

**Every session**

Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity read it first
:::
:::

::: {.bigline}
✍️ say it once → every session follows it
:::

::: {.notes}
`AGENTS.md` is a plain Markdown file in the project folder. Coding assistants read it at
the start of every session, so rules written there survive a restart, a new day and a
catch-up. Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` when the project has no `CLAUDE.md`
(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory); Codex "reads `AGENTS.md` files before doing any
work" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md); Antigravity reads
`AGENTS.md` or `GEMINI.md` in the project root (https://antigravity.google/docs/rules). All
checked 2026-10-30. It is context, not enforcement: the assistant can still slip, so check
the results. Keep it short and checkable; it grows with the project, and the environment
step adds its commands. This workshop's own repository has one too.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
the photo shows with its credit and the link opens TfL.
:::

::: {.notes}
`[text](url)` is a link; `![caption](file)` an image. The `{...}` after the image is a
Pandoc/Quarto extension: `width` sizes it and `fig-alt` is the alt text screen readers
announce (without it the HTML image has no alt). `>` starts a blockquote. The file has
the full alt text: "Big Ben's clock tower and the Palace of Westminster against a blue sky
with white clouds." The assistant copies the photo folder; by hand it is
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/images .`.
Photo: "Big Ben in the sun", John Dillenbeck, CC0 1.0, file page
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Big_Ben_in_the_sun.jpg (licence and absence of
people checked 2026-10-30). The tip: 8 of London's 10 most visited ALVA attractions have free
general admission (`examples/london/data/attractions.csv`). Free tickets: the British Museum
advises booking a free ticket because entry without one depends on capacity, with queues
expected at busier times (https://www.britishmuseum.org/visit); the Natural History Museum says ticket
holders skip the queues and a free entry ticket guarantees entry
(https://www.nhm.ac.uk/visit.html). Both checked 2026-10-30.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 1 min

::: {.done}
every sight has a photo and a working "Read more" link.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pipes `|` separate columns; the `|---|` row marks the header, and its dash counts set the
relative column widths. An image or a link works inside a cell. The light card shows two of
the five rows, one free and one paid, so the text stays readable; the rendered `london.html`
has all five. PowerPoint tables cannot
hold pictures, so the pptx version shows each photo's alt text instead. Photos (credits in
`images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, checked 2026-10-30): British Museum, Mike Peel; Tate Modern and
National Gallery, Diego Delso; Tower of London, Dietmar Rabich (all CC BY-SA 4.0); Natural
History Museum, Julian Herzog (CC BY 4.0); all via Wikimedia Commons, with no people.
"Read more" links are each sight's official visitor page. Check what the assistant
writes: these are facts. Stations from the official visitor pages (checked 2026-10-30):
British Museum, Tottenham Court Road (britishmuseum.org/visit); Natural History Museum,
South Kensington (nhm.ac.uk/visit/getting-here.html); Tate Modern, Southwark
(tate.org.uk/visit/tate-modern); Tower of London, Tower Hill
(hrp.org.uk/tower-of-london/visit/getting-here). The National Gallery's pages name no
nearest Underground station, so that one comes from TfL: a StopPoint search around the
Gallery's coordinates (taken from the Gallery's own TfL map link) lists Charing Cross
Underground first, then Leicester Square and Embankment
(https://api.tfl.gov.uk/StopPoint/?lat=51.50893020629883&lon=-0.12829899787902832&stopTypes=NaptanMetroStation&radius=800);
station page, Bakerloo and Northern lines, Trafalgar Square:
https://tfl.gov.uk/tube/stop/940GZZLUCHX/charing-cross-underground-station. For step-free
access the Gallery suggests Tottenham Court Road or Westminster
(https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/visiting/access).
"Free" means free general admission (ALVA code 4: special exhibitions charged); the
Tower of London is "Paid" (ALVA code 1, all pay).
:::

::: {.done}
`uv run quarto check jupyter` reports the Python in this folder's `.venv`.
:::

::: {.notes}
The next section runs Python, so the guide gets its own environment first, recorded in the
folder: `pyproject.toml` lists the packages, `uv.lock` pins their exact versions, and
`.venv/` holds them. Keep the preview running: `london.md` needs no Python. Quarto needs `ipykernel`, `nbclient`, `nbformat` and `pyyaml` to run
`{python}` cells; the guide adds `pandas`, `matplotlib` and `plotly`. The bigger `jupyter`
package (JupyterLab and Notebook) is not needed. uv installs in seconds: on 2026-10-30 a
cold install of the Part 2 set took 8 s with uv and 31 s with pip plus `jupyter`, on one fast
connection. Quarto
refuses to run Python next to an unactivated `.venv` ("There is an unactivated Python
environment in .venv"), so every Quarto and Python command from here on starts with
`uv run`, which also brings `.venv` up to date from `uv.lock` first; the rule goes into
`AGENTS.md` so the assistant keeps it after a restart. A copied checkpoint
therefore rebuilds its environment on its first `uv run`. Docs, checked 2026-10-30:
https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/run/ and
https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
`london.html` shows the title, author and date.
:::

::: {.notes}
YAML front matter sits between two `---` lines at the very top: `title`, `author` and
`date` make the title block; `format` picks the output. `.qmd` = Markdown + YAML + code.
`date: today` is filled in at render time. Delete `london.md` once `london.qmd` exists:
both would write `london.html`. Two-space indentation matters in YAML. The preview from
the Render step watches `london.md`, so restart it on the new file. Keep `format: html` for
now: the code and figure come next, then all six formats at the end of the block, so each
export carries computed results. Checkpoint 02 is the end of this block, so it is ahead of
this step.
:::

::: {.notes}
A fence with `{python}` runs when you render, and its output lands in the document. Inline
code `` `{{python}} name` `` puts a value in a sentence, so the text never goes stale. The
syntax arrived in Quarto 1.4 (https://quarto.org/docs/blog/posts/2024-01-24-1.4-release/,
"Inline Code Syntax"). Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/computations/inline-code.html (both
checked 2026-10-30). The data folder can also be copied by hand:
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/data .`. The numbers on the light card are
computed by this deck from `examples/london/data/attractions.csv`: ALVA "Visits made in
2025", London rows, top ten (https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423, retrieved
2026-10-30). Only ALVA members are counted, so this is not every London sight.
:::

ldn_short = ldn_att.assign(attraction=ldn_att["attraction"].str.replace(" (South Kensington)", ""))
ldn_ax = ldn_short.sort_values("visits_2025").plot.barh(
    x="attraction", y="visits_2025", legend=False, color="#1f6f8b", fontsize=14,
    figsize=(7.4, 3.8))
ldn_ax.set_xlabel("Visits in 2025", fontsize=14)
ldn_ax.set_ylabel("")

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.done}
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your phone 📱
:::

::: {.notes}
The assistant runs `gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push`, which creates
the GitHub repository from this folder and pushes the commits
(https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create), using the `gh` sign-in from the setup check.
`quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt` skips the confirmation question an assistant cannot
answer (`quarto publish --help`, Quarto 1.6.40); it renders locally, creates the `gh-pages`
branch on its first run, pushes the site and opens it. For a project site no
Settings → Pages change is needed; that page shows the URL and status
(https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html,
checked 2026-10-30). Alternative: a GitHub Action renders on every push using
`quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2` and `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2` with
`target: gh-pages`; run `quarto publish gh-pages` once locally first, and the Action needs
Python and the packages (or `freeze: auto` with `_freeze/` committed). The finished project
is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`; Part 1 has no checkpoint after 04.
:::
